Home/Film & home video

GhostVideo rental stores · Dallas, Texas

Blockbuster

First store opened Oct 19, 1985. Filed for Chapter 11 on Sep 23, 2010.

19852010

It had a store within a short drive of most American homes. Then the drive stopped being necessary.

Blockbuster was the video rental chain that ended 2004 with 9,094 stores in 25 countries and filed for bankruptcy in 2010. Its 2004 revenue was just over $6 billion. That year it borrowed heavily to pay a parting distribution as it left its parent, Viacom, and prepared to give up the late feesBlockbuster’s name for a late fee: a charge when a rental was kept past its due date. Glossary entry that had carried its profits.

What it was

Cause
Technology shift

Key findings

  1. The stores did not empty overnight. Revenue was still $5.07B in 2008, four years after the peak. What collapsed first was profit: the company reported a net loss in every year from 1997 to 2010 except 2006.26910 Sources for this block
  2. It left Viacom carrying debt. Long-term debt went from $75.1M at the end of 2003 to $1,119.7M a year later, after a $1.15B credit facility and $300M of notes paid for a $5.00 a share distribution on the way out.56 Sources for this block
  3. Late fees were a pillar, and it knocked the pillar out. Extended viewing fees were $692.6M in 1999, or 15.5% of revenue. Ending them in 2005 was expected to cost $250M to $300M of operating income a year.25 Sources for this block
  4. It had a credible answer to Netflix, late. Blockbuster Online launched in August 2004 and reached about 2.2 million subscribers by the end of 2006. Netflix had 6.3 million by then.5721 Sources for this block
  5. The name outlived everything else. Dish closed the corporate stores by January 2014. Franchisees carried on, and since 2019 the Bend store has been the only one in the world.272930 Sources for this block

Why ghost

Blockbuster Inc. sold its assets out of Chapter 11 in 2011 and the last corporate stores closed by January 2014, but one franchised store in Bend, Oregon still rents films under the name, and blockbuster.com still shows the logo over a holding page.1327293132 Sources for this block

pets-com.hero:
Home/Dot-com & internet

DeadOnline pet retail · San Francisco

Pets.com

Began operating Feb 17, 1999. Announced its wind-down Nov 7, 2000.

19982000

The company’s slogan was “Because pets can’t drive.” Its business model didn’t get far either.

Pets.com was an online pet store with the most famous mascot of the dot-com era, Amazon as its biggest shareholder and a Super Bowl ad, and it announced its wind-down in November 2000. In 270 days as a public company it never sold a single quarter’s goods for more than they cost to buy and ship.

Cause
Unit economics

Key findings

  1. It lost money before marketing. Cost of goods soldThe costs a company books directly against the products it sells. Whether shipping, warehouse labor and delivery belong here is a choice each company makes and discloses. Glossary entry, including shipping, was higher than sales in every quarter it reported. Its prospectus put shipping costs at 100–110% of revenue.1 Sources for this block
  2. It bought fame, not loyalty. It spent $103.1M on marketing & sales over six quarters against $31.6M in sales.4 Sources for this block
  3. It went public weeks before the crash. The IPO priced on Feb 11, 2000. The Nasdaq peaked on Mar 10.26 Sources for this block
  4. No one would refinance it. Fewer than 8 of the 50+ buyers and investors Merrill Lynch approached would even visit.5 Sources for this block
  5. The idea wasn’t wrong. Chewy did $11.86B in sales in FY2024, built on subscriptions and positive gross margins.19 Sources for this block

Why dead

Pets.com, Inc. was dissolved and liquidated in 2001–2004; pets.com only redirects to PetSmart and nothing trades under the name.61036 Sources for this block

orbitz-drink.hero:
Home/Food & drink

DeadNon-carbonated fruit drink · Vancouver, British Columbia

Orbitz

Launched in 1996. Discontinued by 1999.

19961999

A drink you could chew. Teenagers tried it once.

Orbitz was a non-carbonated fruit drink from Clearly Canadian, the Vancouver maker of flavored sparkling waters, and it had been discontinued by 1999. Its selling point was the small balls of gellan gumA gel-forming hydrocolloid that the Associated Press named as the material of the Orbitz spheres. Glossary entry that hung, without sinking, in the liquid. Launched in 1996 for 12- to 17-year-olds, it sold a million cases in its first months, by the company’s account, and was a hit in 1997. In the first half of 1998 its sales fell by almost 85%. The company said this was the life cycle it had expected; by 1999 the drink was gone. It rests on contemporary press and Clearly Canadian’s own SEC filings.

SP1996–1999

The drink in four numbers

1M

Fact file

What it was
A non-carbonated fruit drink with floating gel spheres, made by Clearly Canadian Beverage Corporation of Vancouver481 Sources for this block
Launched
Introduced in the United States in May 1996, according to Science World in October 1996; the Canadian launch was announced on April 14, 1997, with sales from May 1, 1997 (1996)98 Sources for this block
Highest sales figure found
$9.4M in the first half of 1997, a company figure reported by Strategy in 1998; the article does not name a currency (H1 1997)4 Sources for this block
End
Discontinued by 1999 (Gastro Obscura). A company-history reference says sales were suspended, with a significant writedown, in its account of the fall of 1999; no primary source gives a date. (1999)513 Sources for this block
Company buyer
None: Orbitz was a product, not a company. Its maker filed a proposal to its creditors under Canada’s Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act on March 17, 2010. Fast Company reported in October 2024 that Robert R. Khan acquired the Clearly Canadian company in 2012. (2010 – 2012)2724 Sources for this block
Name owner
No current owner found. The maker’s 2006 application for ORBITZ was abandoned in December 2008, and a 2014 application by a different applicant was abandoned on request. Fast Company reported in October 2024 that the old owners sold the trademark; it did not name a buyer.222324 Sources for this block
What remains
Unopened bottles for collectors: Gastro Obscura says one can sell for around $50 on eBay. Fast Company reported that the machine that made the spheres was sold for parts, and that Clearly Canadian itself resumed full-scale production in 2017.524 Sources for this block
Cause
A fad that faded

Key findings

  1. Built to be talked about, not repeated. Its spokesman said the aim was to make whoever brought Orbitz into a room “the center of attention for a few moments.”1 Reviewers called it a lava lamp, tapioca and worse.12 Sources for this block
  2. The collapse was in the plan. When first-half sales fell from $9.4M to $1.46M, the marketing chief said: “Our expected life-cycle of the product is coming true.”4 Sources for this block
  3. No advertising budget to rescue it. Clearly Canadian relied on product placement, sampling and events, saying advertising was “too mass for our products and, quite frankly, not affordable.”4 Sources for this block
  4. The parent kept shrinking. Clearly Canadian’s revenue fell from $34.9M in 1998 to $20.5M in 2002, with losses in every year after 1998. Its own filings warned that beverage brands may last “a few years” before tastes change.6 Sources for this block

Why dead

Clearly Canadian stopped making Orbitz by 1999 and said in 2015 that it no longer had the equipment to make it. Old bottles sell to collectors; we found no official revival.5 Sources for this block
